nameStory: The "carrionflower" name comes from this plant's truly unforgettable smell - its small green flowers emit a putrid, rotting meat odor that attracts flies and beetles for pollination. The "smooth" part distinguishes it from its prickly cousins in the greenbrier family, as this species typically lacks the thorns that make other greenbriers so memorable to hikers.
description: Smooth carrionflower is a climbing vine that scrambles up through shrubs and trees using curly tendrils, reaching several feet in height. Unlike its thorny greenbrier relatives, this vine has smooth, thornless stems and heart-shaped leaves. In late spring, it produces clusters of small, unremarkable green flowers that pack a punch with their foul smell, followed by dark blue-black berries in late summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish clusters that smell strongly of rotting meat or garbage - the odor is unmistakable and can be detected from several feet away in May and June

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green to reddish stems that are completely thornless - you can run your hand along them without getting scratched, unlike other greenbriers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with prominent parallel veins running from base to tip, feeling smooth and somewhat leathery to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbs using curly, spring-like tendrils that emerge from leaf bases and wrap tightly around nearby stems and branches

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark blue to nearly black berries in small clusters, about the size of large peppercorns, ripening in late summer on female plants

habitat: Look for smooth carrionflower in moist, partially shaded areas like forest edges, woodland clearings, thickets, and meadow borders throughout New England. It thrives in rich, moist soils and often grows as an understory vine, climbing up through shrubs and into the lower branches of trees in deciduous and mixed forests.

seasonality.spring: New heart-shaped leaves emerge in May, followed by the infamous stinky flower clusters that bloom through June - this is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, female plants develop small green berries that gradually darken, while the vine continues climbing and the leaves remain green and prominent.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to dark blue-black and leaves may turn yellow before dropping, making the bare, smooth stems more visible among other vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving no visible trace above ground - this herbaceous vine completely disappears until spring regrowth.

funFact: This plant is nature's master of deception - it mimics the smell of rotting flesh so convincingly that flies will actually lay their eggs on the flowers, thinking they've found the perfect nursery for their maggots!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other greenbriers, but the completely smooth, thornless stems are a dead giveaway - if you can grab the stem without getting pricked, and it smells terrible when flowering, you've found smooth carrionflower.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "greenbrier," this species is often considered the friendly member of the family since it won't scratch you like its thorny relatives that can shred clothing and skin.
compareHints: Unlike roundleaf greenbrier and sawbrier, smooth carrionflower lacks thorns entirely and dies back to the ground each winter rather than remaining woody year-round. The heart-shaped leaves and distinctive carrion smell during flowering also set it apart from other Smilax species, which typically have rounder leaves and less offensive odors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Roundleaf greenbrier stands out from its relatives by its distinctly circular to heart-shaped leaves - sawbrier and saw greenbrier have more elongated, oval leaves.

Among New England's greenbriers, sawbrier stands out for its distinctly pale, whitish leaf undersides - roundleaf greenbrier lacks this feature and has rounder leaves, while smooth carrionflower is herbaceous (not woody) and lacks thorns entirely.
Saw greenbrier differs from roundleaf greenbrier by its distinctly flattened, saw-toothed prickles rather than straight thorns, and its thicker, more leathery leaves.
